name: Periosteal Galvanic Stress Fracture Emitter
description:
The Periosteal Galvanic Stress Fracture Emitter directs a focused beam of low-frequency alternating electrical current through the target's skeletal structure using transcutaneous capacitive coupling — no physical contact required. The current is modulated to exploit the piezoelectric properties of bone mineral, inducing microscopic oscillatory stress at the crystalline level of hydroxyapatite within cortical bone. Over a sustained engagement of thirty to ninety seconds, this mechanical fatigue accumulates until spontaneous stress fractures propagate through weight-bearing bones. The tibia and femur are primary targets at standard settings; the weapon can be retargeted to the spinal column with a firmware adjustment.

The PGSFE-3 differs from earlier galvanic bone-disruption concepts in its use of a resonance feedback loop: onboard sensors detect the acoustic signature of the target's bone structure through the return signal, allowing the emitter to continuously tune its frequency to the target's specific bone density and mineral composition. This means the weapon is self-optimizing — it gets more efficient the longer it is applied. An operator who holds a target in the beam for the full ninety-second cycle will typically induce complete bilateral tibial fracture, dropping the target without any surface wound, blood, or external sign of cause.

The emitter requires line-of-sight but penetrates most civilian clothing without attenuation. Thick metal plating — the kind found in high-end combat chassis augmentations — can shield the underlying biological bone, but few civilian-grade augments include full skeletal shielding. The weapon's power draw is substantial, and the emitter head generates significant waste heat, requiring a thirty-second cooling cycle between full engagements.
specifications:
effective range: 3–20 meters
minimum engagement time: 30 seconds (hairline fracture)
full effect engagement time: 90 seconds (complete fracture)
resonance feedback update rate: 40 Hz
cooling cycle: 30 seconds between full engagements
power source: High-draw galvanic cell, 4 full engagements per charge
weight: 5.8 kg with power cell
form factor: Heavy carbine with large-diameter emitter head
countermeasure: Full skeletal metal plating (military-grade augmentation only)
tactical_use: Deployed in situations requiring incapacitation without lethality — hostage scenarios, high-value capture operations, or crowd control where the political cost of deaths is unacceptable but permanent injury is tolerable. Military units use it to collapse enemy combatants in fortified positions without entering the kill zone. The weapon's weight and cooling requirement make it a two-operator weapon in field doctrine — one holds the emitter, one provides security during the cooling cycle. Some operators use sub-threshold pulses to induce bone pain and fracture risk as a psychological pressure tool without committing to a full engagement.
cultural_context: Among GLMZ's military and paramilitary contractors, the PGSFE-3 is regarded with a particular dread reserved for weapons that produce suffering without death. Soldiers who have been 'crackerjacked' and survived with multiple spontaneous fractures describe the experience as uniquely dehumanizing — bones break from the inside while the skin remains intact. Veterans' advocacy groups in the city have been pushing for the weapon's classification as a torture device under GLMZ's internal security codes, so far without success. Tessera Corponation maintains the PGSFE-3 is a 'minimum force compliance tool.'
story_hooks: A mass casualty event in a transit hub shows forty-seven people with spontaneous bilateral leg fractures and no external wounds — someone used a PGSFE-3 on a crowd, and the only footage shows a maintenance worker with an oversized equipment bag.

A Tessera Corponation engineer who worked on the PGSFE-3's resonance feedback system is trying to defect — she claims the weapon has a classified setting that targets spinal vertebrae and was used in an undisclosed operation.
A fixer is hired to retrieve a stolen PGSFE-3 from a gang that has figured out how to bypass the cooling cycle — making it continuous — but has already used it on two neighborhoods.

The resonance feedback system of a captured PGSFE-3 contains logged bone density profiles from dozens of previous targets — a forensic record of every person the weapon was used on, including several who were reported as natural deaths.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist medical instrument disguised as a weapon — a heavy carbine with an oversized cylindrical emitter head that dominates the front third. The profile is deliberately ungainly, suggesting raw functionality over ergonomic grace. The emitter head is wider than the receiver, creating an unbalanced, top-heavy silhouette that reads as 'dangerous medical device' rather than ballistic firearm.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 118 cm. Emitter head diameter: 12 cm. Receiver depth: 8 cm. Barrel equivalent (emitter bore): 6 cm. Width at grip: 5.5 cm.
physical_description.weight_description: Genuinely hefty — 5.8 kg feels like dead weight in the shoulder, all of it concentrated forward. The power cell mounted low in the stock provides some balance, but the large emitter head still pulls the weapon nose-heavy. Handling requires both upper body strength and deliberate movement; it is not a weapon for spray-and-pray work.
physical_description.primary_material: Titanium-reinforced polymer chassis with aluminum heat-sink ribbing along the emitter housing. The power cell casing is sealed stainless steel. Internal structure incorporates copper windings visible through transparent polymer access panels on the sides.
physical_description.finish: Matte industrial gray with satin-finish aluminum ribbing. The emitter head is anodized charcoal black with faint thermal discoloration marks (browns and purples) radiating outward from the emitter bore — evidence of repeated high-heat cycles. The grip section shows subtle scoring from gloved hands. TESSERA logos are stamped in military block-serif sans-serif on the receiver.
physical_description.color_scheme: Battleship gray primary with charcoal black emitter head. Copper-bronze heat venting creates warm accent lines running vertically down the sides. Minimal red accent striping on the safety lever and power indicator.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer with fine cross-hatching, designed to bite into gloved hands without sawing skin. Cool to the touch, slightly gritty, with a texture that suggests industrial-grade non-slip treatment rather than ergonomic comfort.
distinctive_features: Large cylindrical emitter head with visible thermal scarring and concentric alignment rings etched into the front face
Transparent polymer service panels on both sides revealing copper resonance coils and capacitor arrays
Heat-sink fins running the length of the emitter housing, some discolored from thermal stress
Acoustic return sensor array (three small apertures) arranged in an isosceles triangle on the top of the emitter head
Cooling vent cluster (honeycomb pattern) running along the rear of the emitter housing
Red and amber LED indicator strip on the right side of the receiver (power state, frequency lock, thermal status)
Oversized power cell visible through a reinforced window in the stock — a darkened energy core with faint internal glow
Articulated thermal management collar between emitter and receiver, designed for passive heat dissipation
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: TESSERA CORPORATION stamped in block capitals on the left side of the receiver. Military acceptance mark (crossed wrench and lightning bolt) on the stock beneath a serial plate. Frequency calibration serial beneath the emitter base.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn but meticulously maintained. Thermal scarring on the emitter head is expected and normal. Internal optics and resonance sensors are protected by sealed access panels. No rust or corrosion — military-grade materials show minimal degradation. Grip shows honest wear from use. The weapon has the appearance of a specialized tool that is respected and carefully managed, not casually deployed.
